findings.claim: All 48 practice questions in the unit are typed “20 marks — Extract Analysis”.
findings.truth: 24 of them are whole-novel essays (“In the novel as a whole, explore…”) with no printed extract. Those are part (b), the whole-text essay. Relabelled “20 marks — Whole-Text Essay”. The 24 genuine extract tasks keep the old label.

findings.claim: “Before being sent to the Red Room, Jane confronts Mrs Reed directly: ‘You think I have no feelings…’”
findings.truth: That speech is Chapter 4, weeks AFTER the red-room and just before Jane leaves for Lowood. It looks back on the punishment: “I shall remember how you thrust me back… into the red-room”. The red-room is Chapter 2.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 line 1557 (Ch 4, chapter heading at line 1090; Ch 2 at line 403).

findings.claim: “Mrs Reed orders them to lock her back in, saying ‘she has screamed out on purpose.’”
findings.truth: The line is Abbot's, not Mrs Reed's. Mrs Reed arrives afterwards and thrusts Jane back in. Speaker corrected; the action kept.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 line 656: “‘She has screamed out on purpose,’ declared Abbot, in some disgust.” Mrs Reed enters at line 660.

findings.claim: John Reed “calls her a ‘dependant’”.
findings.truth: Brontë spells it “dependent”. A student copying the misspelling into a quotation loses the verbatim credit.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 line 355: “you are a dependent, mama says”.

findings.claim: Brocklehurst “embodies religious hypocrisy… a theme Brontë returns to with St John Rivers later in the novel.”
findings.truth: St John is not a hypocrite. This unit itself teaches that his “asceticism is real” and that he “genuinely practises what he preaches” (L5), and every mark scheme in the unit calls his faith “cold, dutiful”. Reworded as a contrast, not a repetition.
findings.evidence: L5 content_html of this unit; Gutenberg #1260 Ch 31-35.

findings.claim: “Rochester… detects ‘something of vengeance’ in her nature”.
findings.truth: Rochester never says this. “Something of vengeance I had tasted for the first time” is Jane's own narration in Chapter 4, immediately after she defies Mrs Reed. The other half of the sentence (“not naturally austere”) is genuine Rochester, Chapter 14, and is kept.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 line 1620 (Ch 4) for “Something of vengeance”; line 6347 (Ch 14) for “you are not naturally austere”. “vengeance” appears 8 times in the novel and never in Rochester's mouth about Jane.

findings.claim: “Rochester says he detects ‘something of _____’ in Jane’s nature.”
findings.truth: Same false premise as F7. Stem rewritten to the real speaker and moment; the marked answer (“vengeance”, index 1) is right and unchanged.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 line 1620 (Ch 4).

findings.claim: Flashcard 11: “What quality does Rochester detect beneath Jane’s calm exterior?” → “‘Something of vengeance’ — a fierce, rebellious spirit.”
findings.truth: Same false premise as F7. Stem and answer moved to Chapter 4 and to what the passage actually says: the taste is sweet at first and then “metallic and corroding”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 lines 1620-1622 (Ch 4).

findings.claim: Bertha is “the clothed hyena’ who runs at Rochester with ‘something of vengeance’”.
findings.truth: “Something of vengeance” is Jane's Chapter 4 narration and has nothing to do with the Chapter 26 attack. What Bertha actually does is spring at Rochester and grapple his throat.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 line 1620 (Ch 4); Ch 26 “the lunatic sprang and grappled his throat viciously”. “clothed hyena” is verbatim at line 13589.

findings.claim: Bertha is described as a “mad cat” (L4 body, L4 mark scheme, L4 flashcard, L7 body, L7 mark scheme, and the marked-correct option of L7 knowledge check 2).
findings.truth: “Mad cat” describes JANE, not Bertha. Abbot says it as Jane is dragged to the red-room, and Bessie repeats it about Jane flying at John Reed. Bertha is never called a cat. Replaced with wording the novel does use of her: “the maniac” and “snatched and growled like some strange wild animal”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 line 414 “Hold her arms, Miss Abbot: she’s like a mad cat” (Ch 2, of Jane); line 1120 (Ch 4, of Jane). Bertha: line 13580 “it snatched and growled like some strange wild animal”; line 13596 “The maniac bellowed”.

findings.claim: “Jane leaves Thornfield at dawn… She describes the departure as a kind of death: ‘I had already gained the door; but, reader, I walked back.’”
findings.truth: The quotation is verbatim but from the night before, inside Rochester’s room: Jane reaches the door, turns back, kneels and kisses him goodbye. It is not a description of the dawn departure and says nothing about death.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 line 14709 (Ch 27), followed by “I knelt down by him… I kissed his cheek”.

findings.claim: “Jane describes them [the moors] as ‘a ridge of lighted heath’ — a landscape that is both illuminated and exposed.”
findings.truth: The phrase is Chapter 4 and is not a landscape at all: it is an emblem of Jane’s own mind after she defies Mrs Reed — “would have been a meet emblem of my mind when I accused and menaced Mrs. Reed”. Nothing on the moors is described this way.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 lines 1613-1615 (Ch 4). Only occurrence of “lighted heath” in the novel. The moors chapter is Ch 28, from line 14857.

findings.claim: “Jane describes the moors as ‘a ridge of lighted _____.’”
findings.truth: Same false premise as F13. Stem moved to the real moment; the marked answer (“heath”, index 1) is right and unchanged.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 line 1613 (Ch 4).

findings.claim: Mark scheme for the moors whole-text question rewards “the pathetic fallacy of ‘a ridge of lighted heath’”.
findings.truth: Same false premise as F13. Replaced with a point that is true of the moors chapters.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 line 1613 (Ch 4).

findings.claim: “she immediately divides it equally among all four cousins, keeping only five thousand for herself” (repeated in flashcard 8).
findings.truth: Jane has three cousins — Diana, Mary and St John. The £20,000 is split four ways because Jane keeps a share: £5,000 each. As written the arithmetic gives £25,000.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 line 17850: “Were we not four? Twenty thousand pounds shared equally would be five thousand each”; line 17884 “nephew and three nieces”.

findings.claim: In the moors section: “She tells herself: ‘The more solitary, the more friendless…’”
findings.truth: The line is Chapter 27, spoken at Thornfield as Jane answers her own conscience before she leaves. It is not said on the moors. Reworded so the moment is right.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 lines 14634-14636 (Ch 27).

findings.claim: “What is Brontë’s most famous closing line of the reunion chapter?” (L6) and “Which closing line signals Jane’s voice…” (L8), both answered “Reader, I married him.”
findings.truth: “Reader, I married him” is the OPENING sentence of Chapter 38, the final chapter. It closes nothing. Both stems reworded.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 line 20853 “CHAPTER XXXVIII—CONCLUSION”, line 20856 “Reader, I married him. A quiet wedding we had…”

findings.claim: Two knowledge-check stems name “Component 2 Section A”.
findings.truth: Banned spec-code string. Reworded to “the 19th-century novel question”. Both answers are correct against the spec and are unchanged: part (a) is worth 20 marks, and the section assesses AO1 and AO2 (context and spelling are not assessed here).

findings.claim: Every mark scheme in the unit uses the ladder “Top band (17-20) / Upper band (13-16) / Top band (9-12) / Upper-mid band (5-8) / Lower-mid band (3-4) / Lower band (1-2)”.
findings.truth: “Top band” labels two different mark ranges, and “Upper band” / “Lower band” are off the house ladder. Correct mapping would be Top / Upper-mid / Mid / Lower-mid / Low / Basic. Left unedited: this is the fleet-wide band-ladder relabel already queued as its own work item, and doing 48 of them here would collide with that bulk pass.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT.md house ladder; same defect recorded in english-literature-aqa__blood-brothers and __anita-and-me.

findings.claim: Mark scheme quotes the proposal as ‘my spirit addresses your spirit’.
findings.truth: The novel reads “it is my spirit that addresses your spirit”. The quoted words do not appear contiguously. Teacher-facing text only, so not edited.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1260 line 11671 (Ch 23).

summary: 19 findings to fix (9 HIGH, 10 MEDIUM) plus 2 notes, across all 8 lessons; 51 edits. No lesson was clean. The exam claims are sound for this board - no 30-mark essay, no AQA AO split, no SPaG claim, no open-book claim - and the two exam knowledge checks in L8 are both correctly keyed; the only exam-side faults are three banned 'Component 2' spec codes and 24 whole-text essays mislabelled as extract analysis. The real damage is quotation misattribution: three phrases from Chapter 4 (Jane's outburst at Mrs Reed) were scattered across the unit as Rochester's words, as a description of the moors and as a description of Bertha, and 'mad cat' - which Abbot says of Jane - is taught six times as Bertha's animal imagery, including as the marked-correct option of a knowledge check.
